interactions.label: Which type of firearm continues to fire automatically for as long as the trigger

params.question: Which type of firearm continues to fire automatically for as long as the trigger is kept pressed, and is therefore restricted to military and police use?

answers.text: Bolt-action rifle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A bolt-action rifle is manually repeating — the shooter must cycle the bolt by hand to chamber each new round.

answers.text: Semi-automatic pistol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A semi-automatic (self-loading) pistol fires only one round per trigger pull, even though it cycles the next round automatically.

answers.text: Automatic weapon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An automatic weapon keeps firing continuously as long as the trigger is depressed, which is why its use is restricted to military and police forces.

answers.text: Single-shot musket

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A single-shot weapon like a musket must be manually reloaded after every single shot.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three mechanism categories: single-shot (manual reload every round), repeating (manual or self-loading, one round per pull), and automatic (continuous fire on a held trigger).
Right — continuous fire on a held trigger is the defining feature of automatic weapons, distinguishing them from repeating and single-shot mechanisms.

interactions.label: An investigating officer refers to the entire spent metallic case recovered from

params.question: An investigating officer refers to the entire spent metallic case recovered from the scene as the 'bullet'. Why is this description technically incorrect in a forensic report?

answers.text: The term 'bullet' refers only to the projectile, not the case, primer, or propellant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The bullet is only the projectile component of the cartridge. Calling the whole spent case a 'bullet' is a common but avoidable error in forensic documentation.

answers.text: The term 'bullet' refers only to the case, not the projectile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The case (or shell) is the metallic cylinder that holds the cartridge together — it is distinct from the bullet, which is the projectile itself.

answers.text: 'Bullet' and 'cartridge' are interchangeable in forensic terminology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A cartridge is the complete self-contained round — case, primer, propellant, and bullet together. The bullet is only one of its four components.

answers.text: The term 'bullet' refers to the primer and propellant together

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The primer ignites the propellant, but neither is the bullet — the bullet is the projectile that sits at the open end of the cartridge, ready to be fired down the barrel.

overallFeedback.feedback: Keep the four cartridge parts distinct: case (shell), primer (ignition charge), propellant (produces gas), and bullet (the projectile alone).
Exactly — precise cartridge terminology matters because each of the four components (case, primer, propellant, bullet) contributes differently to recovered evidence and residue.

interactions.label: A 0.22 caliber rifle bullet fired at high velocity produced a more lethal wound

params.question: A 0.22 caliber rifle bullet fired at high velocity produced a more lethal wound than a larger-caliber pistol bullet fired at the same range. What best explains this?

answers.text: Kinetic energy increases with the square of velocity, so the smaller but faster bullet delivered more destructive energy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Since kinetic energy scales with velocity squared, a smaller bullet travelling much faster can transfer more destructive energy than a larger, slower one — caliber is not the same as power.

answers.text: Caliber alone determines the lethality of a gunshot wound, irrespective of velocity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Caliber only describes bullet diameter; it does not by itself predict wounding capacity, which depends heavily on velocity.

answers.text: The pistol bullet must have missed vital structures, which explains the difference

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This assumes an unstated scenario; the narration's point is that velocity, not shot placement, explains why the smaller bullet was more lethal.

answers.text: Recoil force, not bullet velocity, determines wounding capacity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Recoil is the backward force felt by the shooter and can leave powder burns useful in determining self-infliction, but it does not determine the wound's destructive potential.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall that caliber (bullet diameter) is not the same as power. Muzzle velocity drives wounding capacity because kinetic energy scales with velocity squared.
Correct — velocity, not caliber, is the dominant driver of tissue destruction because kinetic energy scales with the square of velocity.

interactions.label: At autopsy, a high-velocity rifle wound to the abdomen shows an entrance hole on

params.question: At autopsy, a high-velocity rifle wound to the abdomen shows an entrance hole only slightly larger than the bullet's diameter, yet the liver and spleen are extensively lacerated well beyond the visible bullet track. What mechanism best explains this pattern?

answers.text: A large temporary cavity from the pressure wave stretched and damaged the surrounding rigid organs beyond the permanent track

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In high-velocity wounds the temporary cavity can balloon to 20–30 times the bullet's diameter, badly damaging rigid organs like the liver and spleen well beyond the permanent track, even though it springs back almost immediately.

answers.text: The bullet must have fragmented into several separate entrance wounds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fragmentation does worsen destruction, but the scenario describes a single small entrance wound, which points to temporary cavitation rather than multiple fragment tracks.

answers.text: The permanent cavity alone accounts for all tissue destruction seen in high-velocity wounds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The permanent cavity is only the crushed track itself; it cannot explain damage well beyond the bullet's path — that requires the temporary cavity's pressure wave.

answers.text: The wound is inconsistent with a rifle and more typical of a shotgun blast

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A shotgun at this range would produce multiple pellet tracks and a ragged entrance, not a single small punched-out hole — this pattern is classic for a high-velocity rifle bullet.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the permanent cavity is the physical track, but the temporary cavity — a brief pressure-wave stretch — can hugely amplify damage to rigid organs in high-velocity wounds.
Exactly — a small entrance with disproportionate internal injury is the hallmark of temporary cavitation from a high-velocity bullet, a finding with real medico-legal weight.

interactions.label: An abrasion collar (Fisch ring) is typically found around exit wounds, formed as

params.question: An abrasion collar (Fisch ring) is typically found around exit wounds, formed as the spinning bullet drags the skin outward while leaving the body.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite — this statement is false. The abrasion collar (Fisch ring) is an entrance wound feature, caused by the spinning bullet scraping the skin as it stretches inward. Exit wounds tear outward and have no abrasion collar.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct, this is false. The abrasion collar forms at the entrance, where the bullet compresses and stretches the skin inward as it punches in. Exit wounds are formed by outward tearing force and characteristically lack an abrasion collar altogether.

interactions.label: During autopsy of a gunshot injury to the head, probing the wound track reveals

params.question: During autopsy of a gunshot injury to the head, probing the wound track reveals a downward path from the vertex of the skull into the neck. What does this trajectory most strongly suggest about the shooting?

answers.text: The shooter was positioned above the victim, which argues against a typical self-inflicted injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A downward track from the vertex into the neck means the shot was fired from above the victim's head — a position that is very difficult to achieve in a self-inflicted shooting, and argues against most self-inflicted scenarios.

answers.text: The shot was fired from a distance greater than 60 cm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Wound track direction (trajectory) tells you the shooter's relative position, not the range of fire — range is instead estimated from blackening, tattooing, singeing, and the abrasion collar.

answers.text: The weapon used was definitely a shotgun rather than a rifled firearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Trajectory alone does not identify the weapon type; a downward track can occur with any firearm fired from an elevated position relative to the victim.

answers.text: The wound is consistent with a horizontal, self-inflicted shot to the temple

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A horizontal track between the right temple and left parietal region is the pattern consistent with a level, self-inflicted shot — a downward vertex-to-neck track is a very different, and more suspicious, finding.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall that the wound track's direction reveals the shooter's position: a downward track from above suggests the shooter stood over the victim, which is inconsistent with most self-inflicted wounds.
Right — probing the wound track for its direction (horizontal, angled, or downward) is exactly how a forensic physician reconstructs the shooter's position relative to the victim.
